newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgarian cabinet expected by mid-January.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgarian cabinet expected by mid-January.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialist party will form a new government by mid-January following the resignation of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, the party's new leader Georgi Parvanov said on Monday.
Parvanov said Socialist leaders had met President Zhelyu Zhelev on Monday morning and he had invited the party to form a new government.
"Consultations are proceeding well and I hope that a strong and succesful team will be formed," Parvanov told reporters.
The leader of the ex-communist Socialists said a party plenum would be held on January 8 with the aim of presenting a cabinet list to Zhelev on January 10.
"If everything proceeds well, I hope that on January 16, parliament will vote on the proposal," he said.
Videnov resigned at a congress of his Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) on December 21, saying he lacked the necessary support to continue as prime minister and party leader.

Zhelev, a staunch critic of the Socialists, said on Sunday the shortcomings of Videnov's government had been obvious a year ago and he regretted that as president of a parliamentary republic he lacked the power to dismiss the cabinet himself.

"If Bulgaria was a presidential republic where the president had the right to appoint and dismiss the prime minister, I would have dismissed Mr Videnov and his government long ago in order to promote more responsible and competent people," Zhelev said in a broadcast on radio and television.
"The current severe economic crisis could have been avoided and our country could have developed in a totally different way."
The ex-communist government's failure to carry out prescribed economic reforms has led to suspension of funding from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank.

The new government, Bulgaria's ninth since the end of one-party communist rule in 1989, will have the task of implementing a currency board, a form of fixed exchange rate regime proposed by the IMF as a last resort to halt the collapse of the lev.

Possible new prime ministers include the speaker of parliament Blagovest Sendov, Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, and U.S.-born former foreign minister Georgi Pirinski, who resigned last month after a party confidence vote gave Videnov only narrow backing.
Zhelev is due to leave office next month and hand over to opposition lawyer Petar Stoyanov, who was elected in November.
